name: Dana Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most days start with my phone buzzing from the interpreting agency at about eight, asking if I can get to a housing office or a clinic by ten. I interpret Arabic and English for people who've just arrived, mostly families sorting out tenancies, doctor visits and school forms, and in the evenings I translate the paperwork, birth certificates and letters, at my kitchen table. I love the moment someone's shoulders drop because they finally understand what the housing officer is saying. What wears me out is the waiting, the unpaid bus rides and the fact that I'm paid by the hour only when I'm actually in the room.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How steady is the work, week to week?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not steady at all. A good week is about twenty paid hours, a bad week is eight, and the agency keeps about a third of what the council pays them. I share a flat with a friend from university, and after rent I usually have less than one month of money put aside, sometimes nothing. There are only two agencies in town that use Arabic interpreters, and both pay about the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: the free translation apps get people into trouble. Last month a man showed me a tenancy letter he'd put through his phone, and it told him he was being evicted when it was only a rent review. I'd keep telling people that a human interpreter is about trust, not just words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, even if AI stays hype, my life is still shaky. The agency cut the hourly rate last spring and called it a market adjustment, and that had nothing to do with robots. I'm one cancelled booking away from asking my brother for rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the clinic and housing jobs and try to get on the council's own list of interpreters, so I'm not losing a third to the agency. I'd also join the interpreters' association, which costs about thirty a year, because they're the only ones pushing back on rates. I won't touch the AI tools; I don't trust where people's private letters end up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, more than scared. It's the same knot in my stomach I've had since I started, the one that comes every time the phone stays quiet on a Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're one cancelled booking away from asking your brother for help. What happens in that moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother works nights at a warehouse and he'd give it to me without a word, which makes it worse. The last time, I paid him back over three months by skipping the bus and walking forty minutes to the clinic. I hate being the one in the family with a degree who still can't cover rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think decides your rate, really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The council puts the contract out to tender, which means the cheapest agency wins, and the agency squeezes us to stay cheapest. So in the end it's a budget line in an office I've never seen. I'd like that budget written to protect the people in the room, the families and us.

say: Free **translation apps** get vulnerable people into real trouble with letters and tenancies.
A human interpreter is about **trust**, not only about getting the words right.
think: My **income** is shaky even without AI, because the agency already cut the hourly rate.
One **cancelled booking** would leave me asking my brother for rent money again.
do: Apply for the **council's own list** of interpreters to stop losing a third to the agency.
Join the **interpreters' association** for about thirty a year to push back on rates.
Refuse to use **AI tools** because of worries about clients' private letters.
feel: **Tired** more than scared, carrying the same knot she has had since starting out.
Quiet Mondays bring back **dread** about rent and owing her brother.
S0.quote: I hate being the one in the family with a degree who still can't cover rent.
fieldNote: Her worry starts from **pay and agency cuts**, not from technology at all.
She frames the problem as a **tender system** that rewards the cheapest agency.
Refusing AI is partly about **client privacy**, which she raises before any job fear.

steps.text: Apply to join the council's own list of Arabic interpreters
Join the interpreters' association and pay the thirty-a-year fee
Keep taking clinic and housing bookings from the agency

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the agency I'd say the council should never send a family into a housing hearing with an app. Online I'd share the stories, the eviction letter that wasn't an eviction, the medicine dose that came out wrong. I'd sign every petition the association puts out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the written side of my work goes first, the birth certificates and school letters I do at night. That's maybe a third of what I earn, and the agency is already asking us to check machine drafts for half the rate. The face-to-face interpreting might hold for a while, but the council will try remote video with an AI voice as soon as it's allowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop doing the cheap checking work, because it pays less than the bus fare some days. I'd push harder for in-person clinic work and ask the hospital directly about a staff interpreter post, even part-time. I'd also cut my phone plan and stop eating lunch out on clinic days, which saves maybe forty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, mostly. It feels like the people who already have the least are being handed a cheaper service, and so am I.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't use AI tools. If the agency only offered checking work, would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm stubborn, not stupid. If checking machine drafts was that or nothing, I'd do it and send every mistake I found to the association. I'd hate every minute, but at least the work would prove something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's an older Kurdish interpreter at the agency who's done this for twenty years and doesn't use email much. He's the one the families ask for by name. I worry he'll be the first one they stop calling, because he's the slowest to answer the app.

say: Councils should never send a **family** into a housing hearing with only an app.
I'd share the **wrong translations** I've seen and sign every association petition.
think: My **written work**, about a third of my income, would go first.
The council would try **remote AI interpreting** for face-to-face jobs as soon as allowed.
do: Turn down **half-rate checking** of machine drafts because it pays less than bus fare.
Ask the hospital directly about a **staff interpreter** post, even part-time.
Cut her **phone plan** and lunches out to save about forty a month.
feel: **Angry** that poorer families and she are both handed a cheaper service.
S1.quote: I'm stubborn, not stupid. If checking machine drafts was that or nothing, I'd do it and send every mistake I found to the association.
fieldNote: She expects to lose about **a third** of her income quickly, which drives the jump in mood.
Her resistance softens under **real money pressure**, though she wraps it in a cause.
She worries more about an **older colleague** than about herself when asked about others.

steps.text: Ask the hospital about a part-time staff interpreter post
Cut the phone plan and lunches out to save forty a month
Log machine translation mistakes and send them to the association

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what everyone would be saying, that nobody voted for this. I'd be at the protests, because if every office job goes in two years then it's not just translators, it's the housing officers I work with too. Publicly I'd demand that people's livelihoods come before company profits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm finished as a translator by 2028. The face-to-face part buys me nothing, because an AI on a tablet can sit in the room as easily as I can. The robots coming later doesn't help me, since I don't lift anything for a living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd go to the job centre and ask what training they pay for, maybe care work or teaching assistant work, where people still want a person. I'd move back in with my mum to save the rent while I retrain. And I'd join whatever union is fighting for an income guarantee, because I couldn't build savings in two years anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panic, honestly. I'd have no money, no plan that I trust and no time, and the thing I trained four years for would be worth nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said care work. The robots for hands-on work come around 2031. Does that change your thinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me about three years, and three years of care work is better than none. But I'd be starting at the bottom again on minimum wage, and then watching the robots come for that too. Retraining for care work at twenty-nine feels like running towards a door that's already closing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum when you moved back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's for a few months, and we'd both know that wasn't true. She'd make up the spare room and not ask questions, and I'd cry in the bus on the way there.

say: **Nobody voted** for this, and livelihoods must come before company profits.
Every office job going in two years hits **housing officers** and many others, not only translators.
think: I'm **finished** as a translator by 2028, in the room or on paper.
Robots coming later **doesn't help** me, because I don't lift anything for a living.
do: Ask the **job centre** within months which care or teaching assistant training it pays for.
Move back in with her **mum** to save rent while retraining.
Join a union campaigning for an **income guarantee**.
feel: **Panic**, with no money, no trusted plan and no time.
**Grief** that four years of training would be worth nothing.
S2.quote: Retraining for care work at twenty-nine feels like running towards a door that's already closing.
fieldNote: She sees **no protection** from in-person work, which is unusual for an interpreter.
The 3-year **robot gap** reads to her as a short reprieve, not a plan.
Moving home is framed as **defeat**, which matters to her sense of having a degree.
Protest and **union action** are her instinct, ahead of any personal strategy.

steps.text: Ask the job centre which care or teaching assistant courses it pays for
Move back into her mum's spare room to stop paying rent
Join the union campaign for a guaranteed income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for governments to act, so there's no excuse. I'd post about public service jobs, like interpreters for courts and hospitals, being kept human by law. I'd be the annoying one in every group chat sending petitions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is just long enough for me to waste them hoping. I know myself; I'd keep doing the clinic jobs until the bookings stopped. I'd probably be out of translation work by 2030, before the full thing even arrives, because the agencies will switch early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give myself one year to get onto a proper course, probably a teaching assistant course at the college, two evenings a week, while still interpreting by day. I'd try to save a little each month, even twenty, which I've never managed. And I'd write to my local councillor every few months about keeping public interpreting human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. It's like knowing the date your lease ends and having nowhere lined up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste the time hoping. What would make you actually start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a friend going first. If Noor from my course started the teaching assistant course, I'd sign up the same week. I don't jump into things alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what would you tell a younger cousin about studying languages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin to study languages only alongside something people need in person, like nursing or teaching. I love languages, but I'd never tell a teenager to bet a career on them now.

say: Five years is **enough time** for governments to act, so there's no excuse.
Court and hospital **interpreters** should be kept human by law.
think: I'd probably **waste the time** hoping and keep taking clinic jobs too long.
Agencies will **switch early**, so translation work ends for me by about 2030.
do: Start a **teaching assistant course** two evenings a week within a year.
Save **twenty a month**, which she has never managed before.
Write to her **councillor** every few months about human public interpreting.
feel: **Heavy**, like a lease ending with nowhere lined up.
S3.quote: I love languages, but I'd never tell a teenager to bet a career on them now.
fieldNote: She knows her **resistance** will cost her time, and says so openly.
She needs a **friend to go first** before she will move.
Her politics turn into **lobbying** for legal protection of public interpreting.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening teaching assistant course at the college
Put aside twenty a month from interpreting pay
Write to her councillor about keeping court and hospital interpreters human

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we should use it to plan, not to pretend it isn't coming. I'd push the association to start a fund for retraining members. Online I'd probably say translators should be first in line for help, because we were hit first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still lose the translating, just later. But I'd be thirty-seven in 2036, which is young enough to have a second career. That's the only one of these pictures where I can imagine being okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on interpreting for the next few years, because the families need it and I need the rent. Around 2028 I'd start a proper teacher training course, since by then I'd have seen which jobs are holding. I'd also go to the association meetings instead of just paying the fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frozen. There's still a knot, but it's one I could untie.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If teaching also changes by 2036, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then at least I'd be with children in a room. A classroom feels safer than a laptop, because children in a room are the last thing a robot would reach. I'm not naive; nothing is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about money in those ten years? You've said it's always thin.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part I don't have an answer for. My rent goes up every year, and the agency rate doesn't. If I'm honest, I'd still be at one month of savings, and that's the real reason my stomach hurts even in the slow picture.

say: Ten years is a **gift** to plan with, not a reason to pretend.
Translators were hit first, so they should be **first in line** for retraining help.
think: I'd still **lose translating**, but at thirty-seven I could build a second career.
Ten years is the only picture where I can imagine being **okay**.
do: Keep **interpreting** for families for the next few years to cover rent.
Start **teacher training** around 2028, once it's clear which jobs hold.
Go to **association meetings** and push for a member retraining fund.
feel: **Uneasy** but not frozen, a knot she feels she could untie.
Still **worried** about money because savings stay at about one month.
S4.quote: A classroom feels safer than a laptop, because children in a room are the last thing a robot would reach.
fieldNote: Time is the only thing that **turns her** from panic to planning.
Even with a decade, her **thin savings** keep her mood from settling.
She now treats **teaching** as a deliberate move, not a fallback.

steps.text: Keep interpreting at clinics and housing offices for rent
Start a teacher training course around 2028
Push the interpreters' association to set up a retraining fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because I'd have no money and no time. What would help is the council or the government paying people like me to retrain, properly, with a weekly income while we study. Advice and websites don't pay rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the families. When I'm gone from that room, a woman who just arrived will be reading her child's hospital letter through a phone, and nobody will notice if it's wrong. A machine can't see when a mother has stopped understanding and is just nodding.

headlineQuote: A machine can't see when a mother has stopped understanding and is just nodding.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old** Arabic–English interpreter working through an agency for clinics and housing offices.
She shares a flat, has under a month **saved**, and borrows from her brother when bookings fall.
She refuses **AI tools** over client privacy and moves only when a friend goes first.
She blames **cheapest-bid contracts** and wants unions and law to keep public interpreting human.
Her mood runs from anxious to **panicked** at two years, easing only with a decade to retrain.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she would have no money, no plan and no time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **retraining** from the council or government with a weekly income while studying.
